title: Writing icons
hook: iconographers pray and fast as they paint

segments.voice: Yesterday, cross and crucifix: a bare cross, or one that carries a figure. Your line was he died, he rose. Which kind did you pass yesterday? Day one thousand three hundred sixty-three.

A small room, early morning. A wooden board sits on the table, coated smooth and white. Beside it, jars of colored powder, an egg, a cup of water, brushes. The painter hasn't eaten breakfast, and won't until the work is done for the day. Before touching a brush, they stand, make the sign of the cross, and pray. Then they sit down and begin, not with a blank idea, but with a pattern handed down for this exact face. No radio. Very little talking. One line, then another. The finished picture will hang in a church or in someone's home, and people will light candles in front of it. Orthodox Christians have a particular word for what this painter is doing. They don't always call it painting. Today: writing icons.
screen: `A WHITE BOARD, AN EGG, A CUP OF WATER.`

segments.voice: Start with the word. Some Orthodox Christians speak of writing an icon rather than painting one. The idea is that an icon is read, like a page. Its faces, hands, colors and gestures follow patterns passed down from earlier icons, so the iconographer isn't inventing a new look for a saint. They're copying out a text faithfully, the way a scribe copies a Gospel. The goal is to hand something on, not to show off a personal style. Next, the prayer. Tradition says the iconographer prays before and during the work, and some keep a fast while they paint. Jesus speaks about fasting in the Sermon on the Mount, telling his listeners to do it quietly, not for show. An icon is meant to be made in that spirit, traditionally without a signature to show off: the hand at work and the heart turned toward God. That's why the line today is painting as prayer. Then, why pictures at all. Orthodox Christians point to the Gospel of John: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." Their reasoning goes like this: once God has a human face, that face can be painted. Not every church sees it this way. Some Protestant churches keep their walls bare, reading the commandment in Exodus: "Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image." Each side takes that text seriously, and they read it differently. Last, the craftsman. In Exodus, God names an artisan called Bezalel and says, "I have filled him with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship." Skill with the hands, counted as a gift of the spirit. Iconographers stand in that line.
screen: `AN ICON IS READ, LIKE A PAGE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: draw something slowly. Find a pen and any scrap of paper. Settle, and breathe. Choose one simple thing in front of you: a cup, a leaf, your own hand. Draw it so slowly that each line takes a full breath. No erasing, no fixing, no judging how it looks. The point isn't a good drawing. The point is attention, one line at a time. If you pray, you can pray quietly before the first line, the way an iconographer does, in whatever words are yours. If you don't, let the slowness itself be the practice. The bell holds the time.
Writing icons. Making a holy image in prayer and fasting, following patterns handed down, so it can be read like a page.

Your line: painting as prayer. Today, pick one ordinary task with your hands, chopping, folding, writing a note, and do it slowly, with your whole attention. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: In Orthodox and Eastern Catholic churches, iconographers traditionally pray before and during their work, may keep a fast, and follow patterns handed down for each saint; the finished icons are blessed and placed in churches and homes for prayer.

fork.reveal: tradition says the iconographer prays first and follows the old pattern. the aim is to hand something on faithfully, not to invent.

trapdoor: what you thought: an icon is just an old religious painting.
what it means: an image made in prayer and fasting, after patterns handed down, to be prayed with and read like a page.
what a scholar hears: "the Word was made flesh." because God took a face, Orthodox Christians say, a face can be painted; and Exodus counts Bezalel's craft as the spirit of God at work.

Editor pass: cut the Colossians 'image of the invisible God' line and its Greek eikon original, match pair, myth item and trapdoor, which repeated day 1352 (iconostasis); the 'why pictures' step now rests on John 1:14 alone. 'Orthodox Christians often speak of writing an icon': some iconographers and scholars prefer 'painting'; the lesson presents 'writing' as a common usage, not the only one. Confirm.
Hook scene (egg tempera, gesso board, fasting, sign of the cross) is a composite illustration of traditional practice; confirm materials and that the prayer-and-fast description is fair.
'Tradition says the iconographer prays before and during the work, and some keep a fast': confirm.
